excerpt: When the islanders of 1920s Saipan mistaken the governor’s new Protestant bride for a Catholic, the food and gifts started flowing. To keep the feasts coming, the governor decided the theological gap between the two faiths was small enough to bridge before breakfast.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
title: The Japanese Governor, the Priest, and the Protestant Bride

short.text: The Japanese governor of the Northern Marianas was a widower. He sailed to Japan, fell for a young woman at an American Protestant orphanage, married her, and sent word ahead to Saipan that he was bringing home a Christian wife. That, he hoped, would spare them a Buddhist ceremony.
The news raced across the Catholic island. Islanders showered the couple with gifts, hoping to win the governor’s favor. Then they learned she was Protestant.

Hans Hornbostel, who later told the story in a Philippine magazine, was at the dinner table. He heard the governor ask what separated Catholics from Protestants, decide the difference was slight, and turn to his wife:

My dear never have the natives brought me such excellent food, and never have they been so kindly disposed towards me. Now it seems that the people are under the impression that you are a catholic and as I have learned by your own answers to my questions that after all there is very little difference between catholic and the protestant faiths, I think that it would be good policy for you to call on the good Padre tomorrow morning and become a catholic.“Rota Days,” Philippine Magazine, 1936.
Hornbostel thought it a joke until he saw her face. The next day the Jesuit priest met him in town, beaming:
Ah, Mr. Hornbostel, you must come with me to the tavern and celebrate over a bottle of beer a great victory.”Philippine Magazine, p. 34. 1936.
A great victory has been won for the governor’s lady will shortly become one of our faith.
A U.S. Marine major, Hornbostel worked for Hawaii’s Bishop Museum in the 1920s and collected latte-period artifacts on Saipan, Tinian and Rota that the war would otherwise have destroyed.

He survived the Death March and a Japanese prison camp in the Philippines. His wife Gertrude came out of internment with Hansen’s disease. He insisted on joining her at the treatment center in Carville, Louisiana, and the two spent years fighting the stigma in the press. He died on Long Island in 1957.
